status: Pilot, written by Claude on 12 November 2026, checked by the translation workers, and deployed to earthfluent.com on 13 November 2026. Polite forms throughout, except where plain against polite is the lesson. The course stores no readings, so the sound lessons are written in kana.

lessons.title: Sounds and Script - The Five Vowels, Part 1
lessons.description: Japanese has five vowel sounds, a, i, u, e, and o, and each is always said the same way. These four words are made of nothing else.

lessons.title: Sounds and Script - Long Vowels, Part 1
lessons.description: Hold a vowel for two beats and it is a different word. Hear obasan against obaasan, and ojisan against ojiisan.

lessons.title: Sounds and Script - The Small Tsu, Part 1
lessons.description: A small っ is one beat of held silence before the next sound, and it changes the word. Hear oto against otto, and kite against kitte.

lessons.title: Sounds and Script - Three Ways of Writing, Part 1
lessons.description: Japanese is written three ways at once: hiragana for native words and endings, katakana for borrowed words, and kanji for meanings.

lessons.title: Patterns - The Verb Never Says Who, Part 1
lessons.description: The verb is the same whoever is going: 行きます. Only the word in front, marked by は, says who.

lessons.title: Patterns - Polite Endings, Part 1
lessons.description: The ending of the verb says whether it happens, and when: ます, ません, ました, ませんでした.

lessons.title: Patterns - Plain and Polite, Part 1
lessons.description: Every verb has a plain form for family and friends and a polite form, ending in ます, for everybody else.

lessons.title: Patterns - Counting Words, Part 1
lessons.description: A number takes a counting word that fits the thing counted: 人 for people, 冊 for books, 匹 for small animals.

lessons.title: Sentence Building - The Verb Comes Last, Part 1
lessons.description: English says I eat sushi. Japanese says I sushi eat: は marks who, を marks what, and the verb closes the sentence.

lessons.title: Sentence Building - Asking a Question, Part 1
lessons.description: Add か to the end of a statement and it becomes a question. Nothing else moves.
words: あなたは日本語を話します。
あなたは日本語を話しますか。
This is the bus to Tokyo.
これは東京行きのバスです。
Is this the bus to Tokyo?
これは東京行きのバスですか。

lessons.title: Sentence Building - Saying No, Part 1
lessons.description: The no is in the verb's ending, at the very end of the sentence: ます becomes ません, and です becomes ではありません.
words: 私は日本語を話します。
私は日本語を話しません。
私は学生ではありません。

lessons.title: Sentence Building - Little Words After, Part 1
lessons.description: Where English puts to, at, with, and by in front of a word, Japanese puts a little marker after it: に, で, と, で.

lessons.title: Sentences in Use - Going Places, Part 1
lessons.description: The verb 行きます, to go, at work in whole sentences. The place is marked by に, and the verb comes last.
words: I am going to the market.
We are going to the beach.
私たちは海に行きます。
Are you going to the party?
パーティーに行きますか。
彼らは東京に行きます。

lessons.title: Sentences in Use - Questions and Answers, Part 1
lessons.description: A question and its answer, side by side. The answer drops か, and a no changes the verb's ending.
words: はい、車を持っています。
No, I do not speak English.
いいえ、英語を話しません。

lessons.title: Sentences in Use - Describing Things, Part 1
lessons.description: The thing, marked by は, then what it is like, then です to close politely.
words: 女の子は背が高いです。

lessons.title: Sentences in Use - Yesterday, Today, and Tomorrow, Part 1
lessons.description: Japanese has no separate future: today and tomorrow both use 行きます, and only yesterday changes it, to 行きました.
words: I went to the market yesterday.
昨日、市場に行きました。
I am going to the market today.
I will go to the market tomorrow.
昨日は行きませんでした。
